rules.description: WordPress Malware Removal signature database. Seeded from real incidents. Extend by appending; never break the schema. Every pattern here is a CANDIDATE signal, not an auto-delete trigger — the LLM verification gate always reads the file in context before action.

meta.author: Aditya Sharma
meta.note: Patterns are POSIX/PCRE fragments intended for grep -E / Python re. Escape appropriately when used in shell.

field_glossary.source: incident = seen in a real cleanup; research = from public security research; incident+research = seen live then generalized
field_glossary.confidence: field-proven = observed in the wild; documented = real, published technique/family; heuristic = broad indicator, verify carefully (higher false-positive risk)

seo_spam_keywords.explanation: Indonesian/Asian gambling, pharma, and replica SEO-spam terms. Presence in page BODY served to bots (but not browsers) is cloaking. Presence in DB post_content/postmeta is content injection.

payload_hosts.explanation: Foreign hosts commonly used to serve cloaked og:image, remote-eval payloads, or redirect targets. A WordPress og:image or script pointing here is almost always malicious.
payload_hosts.allowlist_note: Legit sites DO use cloudinary/workers.dev. Only flag when combined with cloaking (Layer 1) or gambling terms, or when the reference is injected into core/theme/og tags unexpectedly.

cloaking_router.explanation: A PHP file that serves different content to bots/mobile vs desktop. This is the engine of SEO-spam cloaking. Seen as index.php inside webroot shadow folders alongside indexx.php/indexxx.php.

auto_login_backdoor.explanation: Tiny file (often <1KB) that auto-authenticates a visitor as the first administrator. No web-shell fingerprint — commercial scanners miss it. Real sample: bywp.php (535 bytes).
auto_login_backdoor.context_rule: Malicious when found in a loose root file, uploads, or any non-core/non-plugin location. Legit membership plugins use wp_set_auth_cookie inside their own plugin dir — verify location before flagging.

shells.explanation: Web-shell / file-manager fingerprints. Named samples: barbario.php (remote-eval 'Uchiha Terminal'), sumut.php (GYOKKA file manager), biipass.php (elFinder-style uploader).

obfuscation.explanation: Generic obfuscation/code-exec indicators. HIGH false-positive rate in vendor/minified code — never auto-delete on these alone; always LLM-verify.

htaccess_injection.explanation: Malicious rewrite rules, PHP prepend hijack, or handler injection in .htaccess.
htaccess_injection.note: The DirectoryIndex hijack (e.g. `DirectoryIndex wp-ingat.php index.php`) forces a malicious script to run before WordPress for any directory request — the engine behind ?g= query-string SEO-spam cloaking. Real 2026 case.

php_config_persistence.explanation: auto_prepend_file in .user.ini / php.ini / FPM pool loads a payload on EVERY request. Survives file cleanup.

db_injection.explanation: Database-level injection. Check post_content, postmeta, options (esp. autoloaded), usermeta, comments, and redirect tables.
db_injection.note: Distinguish ACTIVE injection (post_content/options serving to visitors) from PASSIVE log records (log tables recording an investigation). Passive is safe; optionally purge to keep scanners quiet.

hidden_admin.explanation: Attacker-created or hijacked admin accounts. Flag emails outside the owner's domain(s), admins created/edited around the breach window, and users with administrator capability not on the known-good list.
heuristics: user_email not matching owner domain allowlist
wp_capabilities contains 'administrator' for an unexpected user_id

malicious_cron.explanation: WP-cron (wp_options.cron) or system cron entries that fetch external URLs, eval, or write files.

webroot_anomaly_filenames.explanation: Filenames in the web root that are never part of stock WordPress or normal plugins.

known_bad_filenames.explanation: Exact filenames observed in real infections. Presence is near-certain malware but STILL verify (an owner could name something coincidentally).

cookie_auth_markers.explanation: Hard-coded cookie/password gates used by shells to authenticate the attacker.

rogue_rest_route.explanation: Unauthenticated REST route with permission_callback __return_true — the 2026 Essential Plugin supply-chain backdoor vector. Lets anyone invoke privileged code (writes, unserialize, option changes).
rogue_rest_route.context_rule: Some legit plugins expose genuinely public endpoints with __return_true. Confirm the callback does something sensitive (file write, unserialize, update_option, user creation) before flagging.

object_injection.explanation: PHP Object Injection — unserialize() on attacker input, the deserialization gadget-chain path to RCE (used by the Essential Plugin backdoor).

wp_config_injection.explanation: Malware appends executable code to wp-config.php AFTER the wp-settings require. Survives core reinstall because wp-config is preserved (Essential Plugin injected ~6KB there).
wp_config_injection.context_rule: Nothing executable should appear after `require_once ABSPATH . 'wp-settings.php';` in wp-config.php. Anything there is highly suspicious.

persistent_admin_creator.explanation: Code that recreates a rogue admin on every page load — the reason malware 'comes back' after user deletion. ~49% of compromised sites carry a backdoor like this.
persistent_admin_creator.context_rule: Membership/registration plugins legitimately create users inside their own dir. Flag when in a loose/root/uploads file, theme functions.php, or paired with hardcoded credentials.

remote_loader.explanation: Fetches a payload from a remote image/text file (the metainfo.jpg pattern) or a base64-encoded C2 host and executes it. C2 may be resolved indirectly (base64, DNS, even smart contracts).

ssh_key_backdoor.explanation: Attacker SSH public key planted for persistence.
ssh_key_backdoor.context_rule: Legit inside the owner's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. Flag any ssh-rsa/ed25519 string found under the web root, or keys added in the breach window.

cryptominer.explanation: Browser or server-side cryptocurrency miner hijacking CPU.

card_skimmer.explanation: Magecart-style JS that captures checkout/card fields and exfiltrates to an external host (usually WooCommerce checkout).
card_skimmer.context_rule: Payment gateways legitimately read card fields client-side. Flag only when the captured data is sent to a host that is NOT the site's own payment processor.

sitemap_injection.explanation: Rogue sitemap files listing thousands of spam URLs; robots.txt pointed at spam sitemaps (Japanese/gambling keyword hack).
sitemap_injection.note: Compare against the legit SEO plugin's sitemap. Rogue ones contain gambling/pharma URLs or thousands of unrelated slugs. Also check robots.txt for injected Sitemap: lines to foreign hosts.

core_filename_typosquat.explanation: Filenames that mimic WP core files but are not core (extra letter/plural/hyphen). Real sample: wp-comments-posts.php (core is the SINGULAR wp-comments-post.php). Also the wp-vcd family.

double_extension_files.explanation: PHP hidden behind an image/hidden extension so it looks like a harmless upload.

php_stream_wrapper.explanation: PHP stream-wrapper abuse: a compressed/encoded payload hidden in an image or blob, executed via a wrapper. Real 2026 case (r/ProWordPress): malware cloaked as wpengine_update() ran compress.bzip2://screenshot.webp — a compressed PHP payload inside a .webp. Invisible to file scanners because the executable isn't PHP on disk. Sucuri and WP Engine both failed to find it.
php_stream_wrapper.context_rule: phar:// and php://filter appear in some legit libraries. Flag when combined with an image/data source, an option-built path, or an execution sink (include/eval/load_template).

fake_core_function_loader.explanation: Malware declares a legit-sounding function (wpengine_update, wp_cache_init, etc.) guarded by function_exists, builds a file path from wp_options data (keyed by the theme stylesheet), then load_template/locate_template's it — often through a stream-wrapper protocol. Cloaks as host/plugin code and rebuilds itself from the DB (survives file cleanup).
fake_core_function_loader.context_rule: The tell is a file path CONSTRUCTED from database/option content and passed to a loader — legit themes hardcode template paths, they don't build them from options + a protocol wrapper.

wp_vcd.explanation: wp-VCD — one of the most widespread WordPress malware families. Injects a loader into theme functions.php that installs itself across all themes and drops wp-vcd.php / wp-tmp.php / wp-feed.php.
wp_vcd.context_rule: The wp-vcd loader is usually the first lines of a theme's functions.php and references an install hash + a remote content URL.

malicious_js_injection.explanation: Injected JavaScript used for redirects, ad fraud, skimming, or crypto-mining (Balada Injector and similar mass campaigns). Often stored in wp_options, posts, or theme header/footer.
malicious_js_injection.context_rule: Minified/legit libraries can contain fromCharCode/atob. Flag when the destination is an unfamiliar low-reputation TLD, or the JS is injected into wp_options / posts / theme header-footer.

spam_link_injection.explanation: Hidden link farms injected into content or theme — pharma/gambling/replica links hidden with CSS so visitors don't see them but search engines do.
spam_link_injection.context_rule: Hidden text has rare legit uses (skip links). Flag when it wraps outbound links to unrelated commercial/pharma/gambling domains.

dynamic_code_exec.explanation: Dynamic code execution driven by user input — the mechanic behind most PHP backdoors beyond a plain eval().
dynamic_code_exec.context_rule: extract() and call_user_func appear in some frameworks — flag when the argument is a raw superglobal.

gzinflate_layered.explanation: Layered decompress/decode chains and error-suppressed execution used to hide payloads.

polyglot_file.explanation: A file that starts with image magic bytes (so upload filters accept it as an image) but contains PHP — an image/PHP polyglot shell.
polyglot_file.context_rule: Detect on files whose bytes contain both an image header and <?php. Real images never contain <?php.

phishing_kit.explanation: Phishing pages hosted on the compromised site (bank / webmail / brand login clones) that steal credentials.
phishing_kit.context_rule: Brand names + a login form + POST-to-mail/exfil in an unexpected directory = phishing. A legit login form on the site's own domain is fine.

mailer_spam.explanation: Spam-mailer scripts that abuse the server to send bulk email (used for phishing delivery and blackhat SEO).
mailer_spam.context_rule: Contact forms send mail legitimately. Flag loose mailer scripts in uploads/root, or code that mails a list from user input.

ajax_backdoor.explanation: A backdoor exposed through WordPress AJAX — a nopriv AJAX action wired to file/exec/eval, callable by anyone (no login).
ajax_backdoor.context_rule: Many plugins use wp_ajax_nopriv legitimately — flag when the callback runs eval/file-writes/system on user input.

japanese_charset_spam.explanation: Japanese/CJK characters injected into post titles/content/meta — the classic Japanese keyword hack fingerprint. Applied to DATABASE content (Layer 9), not arbitrary files.
japanese_charset_spam.context_rule: Only meaningful on sites that are NOT legitimately Japanese/CJK. Check post_title/post_content/meta; a Japanese-language site matches legitimately. Not run against source files by default.

suspected_files.explanation: Files a host security tool renamed to .suspected (quarantined malware) — review and remove after confirming.
